title: The Blaschka Object Network — Harvard Receiving, Unpacking and Installation Labor Register
scope: Direct Blaschka/Harvard evidence for the skilled work performed after fragile glass models reached the receiving institution: outer handling, customs-supervised opening, unpacking, support removal, repair, remounting, setting-up, installation and public demonstration. The register keeps legal authority, material handling skill, paid technical service, patron participation and curatorial work distinct.
core_guard: Do not collapse all receiving actors into a generic museum technician. The customs inspector possessed opening/inspection authority; E. A. Snow coordinated papers and inspection; porters handled outer packing and internal movement; Mary Lee Ware, Goodale, Waugh and Bierweiler possessed different forms of handling/mounting skill. 'Receiving-side craft' and 'serial reassembly' are project analytical terms. 'Professionalization' is too strong unless employment structures are independently demonstrated.

analytical_observations: Unpacking was not simply packing in reverse. Packing created a temporary transport assemblage; receiving work dismantled that assemblage, inspected condition, removed temporary supports, repaired as necessary, remounted the model, labelled it and installed it for use/display.

Receiving expertise was distributed across actors with non-equivalent powers. Legal authority to open, physical skill to handle, curatorial authority to install and financial responsibility for the work could belong to different people.

Handling knowledge became increasingly explicit in the archive: maker trust in Ware's manual skill; embodied risk advice; a paid Waugh service receipt; a budget describing preservation/installation expertise; and Bierweiler's later assistant/technician role.
Public demonstrations in 1894 and 1906 show that unpacking itself could become an epistemic spectacle: spectators were invited to witness the conversion of shipped glass into museum objects.

The safest longitudinal claim is differentiation, naming, payment and institutionalization of receiving expertise. A linear story of professionalization would overstate the evidence and import later registrar/conservator categories.
